transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A historic railway station in Yorkshire has resumed steam train services for the first time in over fifty years, attracting thousands of visitors on its opening weekend. The restored line, which runs for twelve kilometers through the countryside, was brought back to life by a team of over two hundred volunteers who spent seven years repairing tracks and restoring vintage carriages. The first train, pulled by a 1920s steam locomotive named "The Yorkshire Queen," carried two hundred passengers on its maiden journey Saturday morning. Local businesses report a significant increase in customers, with hotels and restaurants fully booked for the coming month. The service will operate every weekend until October, with special holiday rides planned for Christmas. Organizers say they hope the heritage railway will become a major tourist attraction, supporting local jobs and preserving industrial history for future generations.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: A growing number of elementary schools across Canada are introducing meditation and mindfulness programs to help students manage stress and improve concentration. The programs, which typically involve ten to fifteen minutes of guided breathing exercises and quiet reflection at the start of the school day, have shown promising results in early studies. One school district in British Columbia reported a twenty-five percent reduction in disciplinary referrals and a fifteen percent improvement in test scores after implementing the program for one year. Teachers say students are better able to focus on lessons, handle conflicts peacefully, and regulate their emotions. Parents have also noticed positive changes at home, with children sleeping better and showing less anxiety about schoolwork. While some critics argue the programs take time away from academic instruction, supporters point out that improved mental health actually enhances learning ability.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.

4. What is the main criticism of these programs?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: The city of Manchester has announced plans to expand its successful bicycle sharing program, adding five hundred new bikes and one hundred additional docking stations over the next year. The expansion will extend coverage to suburban areas that currently have no bike share access, making the service available to an estimated additional one hundred thousand residents. City officials say the program, which launched three years ago with three hundred bikes, has already reduced car traffic in the city center by eight percent and increased cycling for commuting by thirty percent. The new bikes will include electric-assist models to help riders tackle hills and longer distances, and a mobile app will be updated to show real-time availability and suggest routes. The project is being funded through a combination of government grants and advertising partnerships, with no additional cost to taxpayers.
Questions 5 to 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.

6. What reduction in city center car traffic has the program already achieved?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Tom): Hey Lisa, have you started planning your summer vacation yet?
Woman (Lisa): Hi Tom, I'm trying to decide between going to the beach or visiting my grandparents in the mountains.
Man: That's a tough choice. The beach is great for swimming and relaxing, but the mountains sound nice too with cooler weather and hiking.
Woman: Exactly. My grandparents have a cabin on a lake, so we can go fishing and boating there. But I also love surfing, and I haven't been to the beach in two years.
Man: How long do you have for vacation? Maybe you could do both?
Woman: I have three weeks total. But if I split the time, I'd only get ten days at each place, and traveling between them would take a whole day each way.
Man: That's true. What does your family want to do?
Woman: My parents are leaning toward the mountains because they want to see my grandparents. But my sister really wants to go to the beach.
Man: Have you looked at costs? The beach might be more expensive with hotel rooms, whereas staying with grandparents would be free accommodation.
Woman: That's a good point. The cabin is free, and my grandma cooks amazing meals, so we'd save a lot on food too. But I was really looking forward to learning to surf this summer.
Man: You could always take a surf lesson some weekend before or after vacation. Or maybe ask if one of your friends who lives near the beach could have you visit for a few days later in the summer.
Woman: That's a great idea! My friend Jake's family has a beach house, and he invited me last year. I could go there for a long weekend in August.
Man: Perfect! Then you get the best of both worlds. How will you get to the mountains?
Woman: We're planning to drive. It takes about six hours, but we can stop along the way at some scenic spots.
Man: That sounds nice. Road trips can be fun. Will you bring your bike?
Woman: Definitely! There are great biking trails around the lake. And my grandpa just got a new kayak too, so I'm looking forward to trying that out.
Man: Sounds like you'll have a wonderful time. I'm just staying home this summer and working at the café to save money for next year's tuition.
Woman: That's responsible of you. But you should take at least a few days off to do something fun.
Man: I will. My roommate and I are planning a day trip to the water park next month.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. What are the two options the man is considering for vacation?
9. Why does going to the mountains save money?
10. How long does it take to drive to his grandparents' place?
11. What is the woman planning to do most of the summer?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Anna): Hi Chris, I just signed the lease on the new apartment. Do you have time to help me think about furniture?
Man (Chris): Of course, Anna! I love decorating. What do you need so far?
Woman: Well, the place is unfurnished, so I need basically everything - a bed, a sofa, a table for eating, and a desk for studying.
Man: That's quite a lot. What's your budget like? Buying everything new can get expensive.
Woman: I know. I'm trying to spend as little as possible since rent is already pretty high. I was thinking about checking secondhand stores and online marketplaces.
Man: That's smart. You can find really nice used furniture for a fraction of the original price. I got my dining table from a charity shop for only twenty-five pounds, and it's solid wood.
Woman: Wow, that's a great deal. What about a mattress though? I feel like I should buy a new one of those.
Man: You're absolutely right. A mattress is something you don't want to buy used - for hygiene reasons. But you can get affordable new ones from discount stores or online retailers.
Woman: Good to know. What about seating? I need something comfortable for when friends come over to watch movies.
Man: A futon could be a good option - it works as both a sofa and a guest bed. Or you could look for a secondhand sofa and just get a new cover for it.
Woman: A futon makes sense because I don't have a guest room. What about storage? The apartment doesn't have a lot of closet space.
Man: You can get inexpensive plastic storage bins that fit under the bed, or maybe a bookshelf that doubles as a room divider since it's a studio apartment.
Woman: It's actually a one-bedroom, but the bedroom is small. A bookshelf divider would be nice to separate the living area from the sleeping area.
Man: Definitely. Also, check if any friends or family are getting rid of furniture. When I moved, my cousin gave me a desk and my neighbor gave me two chairs.
Woman: That's a great point. I'll ask around. I also need kitchen stuff - plates, pots, pans.
Man: Those are easy to find at charity shops too, or you can get a basic set pretty cheaply at a home goods store. Make a list of what you need in order of priority so you don't get overwhelmed.
Woman: I will. Thanks for your help, Chris. Want to come with me to look at some furniture shops this weekend?
Man: Sure! I love browsing furniture stores, even if I'm not buying anything.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: What was once considered vandalism is now recognized as a legitimate art form that transforms public spaces and gives voice to communities. Street art - including murals, graffiti art, stencil work, and installations - has moved from city walls and subway cars into galleries, museums, and auction houses over the past four decades. Artists like Banksy, Shepard Fairey, and JR have achieved international fame, their works selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The roots of modern street art can be traced back to the graffiti movement of 1970s New York City, where young people began writing their names or "tags" on subway trains and buildings as a form of self-expression and territorial marking. Unlike traditional graffiti, which often focused on lettering and identity, contemporary street art typically includes images and messages that comment on social issues, politics, and culture. Many street artists use their work to address topics like inequality, environmental protection, and human rights, bringing important conversations directly to public spaces where people encounter them in their daily lives.

Cities around the world have responded to street art in different ways. Some continue to treat all unsanctioned public art as vandalism, imposing fines and even jail time for offenders. Others have embraced it, creating designated street art districts, commissioning murals from local and international artists, and hosting annual street art festivals that attract tourists and support local businesses. Research has shown that well-planned street art programs can reduce blight, discourage illegal graffiti, increase foot traffic to local businesses, and build community pride. When residents are involved in choosing what art appears in their neighborhoods, street art becomes a powerful tool for community engagement and cultural expression.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: You've probably heard that breakfast is the most important meal of the day, but many people still skip it due to busy schedules, lack of appetite in the morning, or the belief that skipping meals helps with weight loss. Research shows, however, that eating a nutritious breakfast provides numerous benefits for both physical health and cognitive function, especially for students and working adults.

After seven to nine hours of sleep, your body has gone an extended period without food. Eating breakfast kick-starts your metabolism, helping your body burn calories throughout the day rather than conserving energy because it thinks food might be scarce. Studies have found that people who eat breakfast regularly are less likely to be overweight, as they tend to make better food choices throughout the day and experience less extreme hunger that leads to overeating at lunch or dinner.

For students, breakfast has a particularly strong impact on academic performance. Glucose from breakfast provides the brain with its primary fuel source, improving concentration, memory, problem-solving abilities, and attention span. Research conducted in schools has consistently shown that students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, have better attendance, participate more in class, and exhibit fewer behavioral problems than peers who skip the morning meal. Even a simple breakfast like whole-grain cereal with fruit or oatmeal provides lasting energy that prevents the mid-morning energy crash that comes from eating sugary pastries or no breakfast at all.

A healthy breakfast doesn't need to be large or time-consuming to prepare. Options like Greek yogurt with nuts, a piece of fruit with peanut butter, or a vegetable omelet provide protein, fiber, and healthy fats that keep you full and focused until lunchtime. Making breakfast a priority - even if it means preparing something the night before - is an investment in your daily health and performance.

20. What academic benefit is associated with eating breakfast?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Participating in team sports during childhood and adolescence provides benefits that extend far beyond physical fitness, shaping important life skills and character traits that last well into adulthood. While individual sports teach self-reliance and personal discipline, team sports offer unique lessons in collaboration, communication, and collective responsibility that are difficult to learn elsewhere.

One of the most important skills developed through team sports is teamwork itself - learning to work with people who have different personalities, strengths, and weaknesses toward a common goal. Athletes learn to trust their teammates, communicate effectively both verbally and non-verbally, and understand how their individual role contributes to the group's success. These skills translate directly to the workplace, where employees must collaborate on projects, coordinate with different departments, and support colleagues to achieve organizational goals.

Team sports also teach resilience and how to handle both victory and defeat gracefully. In sports as in life, you don't always win, and losing teaches important lessons about perseverance, analyzing mistakes, and working harder to improve. Winning, meanwhile, teaches humility and the importance of sharing credit with others. These experiences build emotional maturity that helps people navigate the challenges of adult life, from career setbacks to personal difficulties.

Leadership skills are another valuable outcome of team sports participation. Many players have opportunities to captain their team, lead warm-ups, or help coach younger players, developing decision-making skills, confidence, and the ability to motivate others. Research has also linked team sports participation to higher self-esteem, lower rates of anxiety and depression, and stronger social support networks. The friendships formed through team sports often last for decades, providing a sense of belonging and community that supports mental health throughout life.
